lesson.title: AWS ECS Fargate and ECR
lesson.why: A container image is not a running service. Deployment also needs scheduling, network reachability, distinct permissions, readiness, and enough spare capacity to replace unhealthy tasks.
lesson.what: Trace an immutable image from ECR into an ECS service on Fargate using an offline deployment specification and failure timeline.

concepts.name: Registry and scheduler differ
concepts.body: ECR stores container artifacts; ECS schedules tasks from task definitions. Fargate supplies managed task compute rather than customer-managed EC2 hosts. Pinning an image digest makes a deployment artifact explicit; reusing a mutable tag can obscure what actually changed.

concepts.name: Two roles solve different problems
concepts.body: The task execution role supports platform operations such as applicable image pulls and log delivery. The task role supplies credentials to application code for its AWS calls. Granting S3 access only to the execution role does not authorize application reads.

concepts.name: Tasks need a network path
concepts.body: Fargate tasks use task networking with security groups and subnet placement. Image retrieval, secrets, logs, and application dependencies need suitable routes or supported endpoints. A private subnet alone neither grants service access nor ensures all startup dependencies are reachable.

concepts.name: Services reconcile healthy capacity
concepts.body: An ECS service maintains desired tasks and coordinates deployments. Container health and load-balancer health observe different paths. Deployment minimum and maximum percentages influence overlap, but quotas, IP addresses, and dependency capacity can prevent replacements from becoming ready.

e2e: Identify a tested image digest and compatible task CPU, memory, and architecture.
Separate application permissions from execution permissions in the task definition.
Trace private network paths for image pulls, logs, secrets, and downstream APIs.
Plan healthy deployment overlap and readiness before draining old tasks.
On failure, inspect task events and roll back the artifact or configuration with evidence.

tasks.name: Map deployment objects
steps: Draw ECR image, task definition, task, and service; label which stores bytes and which maintains desired count.
Explain why pushing a new tag alone does not prove the running service changed.

tasks.name: Calculate deployment overlap
steps: Assume desired count four, minimum healthy 100%, and maximum 150%. Expected lower healthy count is four and upper running/pending count is six.
Only two extra task slots exist in this simplified rollout; reserve subnet addresses and downstream capacity accordingly.

tasks.name: Diagnose role confusion
steps: A task starts and writes logs but its application gets AccessDenied reading S3.
Inspect the task role and resource policy, not merely image-pull permissions. This mock does not prove real IAM evaluation.

tasks.name: Plan a failed rollout
steps: New tasks fail image retrieval while old tasks remain healthy. Check digest existence, execution permissions, and network reachability before replacing working tasks.
Draft rollback to the known task-definition revision and a stop condition for falling healthy count.

key_terms: Task definition: versioned container execution specification.
Task role: permissions used by application code.
Execution role: permissions for platform startup operations.
Digest: content-addressed image identifier.
Desired count: service's target task population.
lesson.safety: Do not push images or run tasks. Fargate runtime, ECR storage, logs, load balancers, and NAT can cost money; never bake credentials into an image.
cleanup: Future tests must remove services, task revisions as appropriate, images, and retained logs separately.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a Fargate task pulls its image successfully but cannot read its configuration object. What do you investigate?
interview_points: Distinguish execution role from task role.
Inspect resource policies and actual caller context.
Verify the application's network path.
Avoid broad grants and preserve a known-good revision.

aws-platform/aws-ecs-fargate-and-ecr.core: ECR stores images, ECS reconciles tasks, and Fargate provides compute. Application permissions belong to the task role, not merely the execution role. Pin digests and budget healthy deployment overlap.

storyboard.title: An ECS task starts but lacks data access
storyboard.objective: Separate image retrieval from application authorization.

scenes.title: Start the task
scenes.caption: Execution permissions enable image retrieval.
scenes.narration: The platform retrieves the pinned image and starts the container using the task definition's execution configuration.

scenes.title: Application request denied
scenes.caption: Startup success does not grant application access.
scenes.narration: The running code requests its configuration object, but the task role lacks the required narrowly scoped permission.

scenes.title: Correct the application scope
scenes.caption: Review the task role rather than widening startup access.
scenes.narration: An approved task-role correction and resource-policy check restore the configuration path while retaining the immutable image.

lesson.title: AWS EKS cluster operations
lesson.why: A managed Kubernetes control plane does not operate every workload or node for you. Cluster upgrades and scaling can fail through networking, add-ons, disruption limits, or application assumptions.
lesson.what: Build an EKS operations plan that separates AWS infrastructure, Kubernetes scheduling, identity, and workload availability. Use manifests and arithmetic on paper, not a real cluster.

concepts.name: Responsibility crosses layers
concepts.body: EKS manages its control-plane service; customers still choose compute options, workload policies, add-ons, and application configuration. Managed node groups automate parts of node lifecycle but do not guarantee every workload tolerates node replacement or supported-version changes.

concepts.name: Pod readiness is not node readiness
concepts.body: A healthy node can host a failing pod. Resource requests guide scheduling, limits constrain usage, and readiness controls service endpoints. Subnet IP availability and CNI configuration can block pod creation even when aggregate CPU appears sufficient.

concepts.name: AWS and Kubernetes permissions differ
concepts.body: Kubernetes RBAC authorizes Kubernetes API actions. AWS IAM authorizes AWS service actions; workload identity mechanisms such as EKS Pod Identity or IRSA connect supported workloads to roles. A Kubernetes service account does not inherently grant S3 or KMS access.

concepts.name: Upgrades need compatibility evidence
concepts.body: Review supported version paths, deprecated APIs, add-on compatibility, and node images before upgrading. Pod disruption budgets constrain voluntary evictions but cannot prevent involuntary failures. Recovery options and rollback support evolve, so verify current EKS documentation rather than assuming arbitrary downgrades are available.

e2e: Inventory cluster version, compute, add-ons, workload owners, and network capacity.
Check deprecated API use and test workload behavior against the intended supported version.
Ensure spare schedulable capacity and disruption settings allow node replacement.
Update components in a documented compatible sequence while monitoring readiness and errors.
Pause on failing gates and use the documented recovery path rather than improvising a downgrade.

tasks.name: Assign responsibility
steps: List API-server availability, application readiness, node image updates, CNI IP capacity, and database backups.
Assign each an operational owner; managed control-plane operation does not eliminate the other responsibilities.

tasks.name: Calculate eviction allowance
steps: A deployment has five healthy replicas and a disruption budget minAvailable of four. The modeled voluntary disruption allowance is one.
If one replica is already unavailable, the allowance is zero. This does not stop an unexpected node failure.

tasks.name: Diagnose pending pods
steps: Given sufficient node CPU but pod sandbox creation failures, inspect subnet IP exhaustion and CNI events.
Distinguish scheduling failures from networking setup failures; a bigger CPU instance may not repair an address shortage.

tasks.name: Write an upgrade gate
steps: Require deprecated-API review, compatible add-ons, representative tests, spare capacity, and service-error thresholds before rollout.
Document the current provider-supported recovery procedure. These offline checks do not establish live Kubernetes or IAM behavior.

key_terms: CNI: integration providing pod networking.
RBAC: Kubernetes API authorization rules.
PDB: budget constraining voluntary pod disruption.
Node group: managed collection of worker instances.
Workload identity: binding workloads to cloud credentials without static keys.
lesson.safety: Do not create or upgrade a cluster. Control plane, worker, load-balancer, storage, and logging costs persist independently; never drain shared nodes for practice.
cleanup: Keep the upgrade checklist and synthetic budget calculation.
Future test cleanup must inspect persistent volumes and load balancers after cluster removal.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, an EKS node rollout stalls despite spare CPU. Which non-CPU constraints would you investigate?
interview_points: Inspect disruption budgets and unhealthy replicas.
Check subnet IP and CNI capacity.
Review affinity, taints, storage, and add-on compatibility.
Use documented recovery rather than assuming unrestricted downgrade.

aws-platform/aws-eks-cluster-operations.core: EKS operations span managed control plane, compute, networking, add-ons, and workloads. Validate compatibility and disruption headroom, distinguish RBAC from IAM, and check IP capacity before blaming CPU.

storyboard.title: An EKS node rollout is blocked by availability rules
storyboard.objective: Connect disruption budget and replacement readiness.

scenes.title: One replacement allowed
scenes.caption: Healthy replicas provide a small disruption allowance.
scenes.narration: The rollout requests a bounded eviction while sufficient ready replicas remain to satisfy the application's disruption budget.

scenes.title: Another replica fails
scenes.caption: The allowance can fall to zero.
scenes.narration: An unrelated unready replica consumes availability headroom, causing further voluntary evictions to pause rather than silently ignoring the budget.

scenes.title: Restore readiness first
scenes.caption: Healthy replacement capacity reopens the gate.
scenes.narration: Operators fix readiness or capacity constraints, then resume the compatible node rollout while watching application errors and scheduling events.

lesson.title: AWS Route 53 and CloudFront
lesson.why: DNS answers and cached content have independent lifetimes. A successful origin deployment can coexist with stale pages, cached failures, or clients still using an old endpoint.
lesson.what: Trace Route 53 name resolution into a CloudFront distribution, then through cache-key selection and origin access. Model changes offline without editing public DNS.

concepts.name: DNS routes names, not HTTP paths
concepts.body: Route 53 answers DNS queries using configured record and routing policies. Resolver caching means changes are not instantly observed by every client. Health-aware routing can change answers, but it cannot close an existing client connection or override every cached answer.

concepts.name: The cache key determines sharing
concepts.body: CloudFront caches according to distribution behavior and cache policy. Selected headers, cookies, and query strings affect whether requests share an object. Omitting a user-specific dimension can leak personalized content; including unnecessary dimensions can destroy the hit rate.

concepts.name: Freshness is a contract
concepts.body: Origin cache headers interact with configured minimum, default, and maximum TTLs. A positive minimum TTL can cause caching despite restrictive origin directives. Versioned asset URLs avoid ambiguity during releases; invalidation removes cached objects but does not replace sound cache-key design.

concepts.name: Origins need deliberate protection
concepts.body: A private S3 origin can use supported origin-access controls and a restricted bucket policy. Custom origins have different access and TLS requirements. Cached error responses, origin timeouts, and stale-content policies require explicit observability so edge success does not hide an unhealthy backend.

e2e: Resolve the public hostname and identify the distribution reached by clients.
Match the request path to a behavior and compute which inputs enter its cache key.
On a miss or expiry, contact the authorized origin and apply response caching rules.
During release, publish versioned assets and control mutable-document freshness.
Diagnose DNS, cache, and origin failures separately before choosing invalidation or routing changes.

tasks.name: Draw two lifetimes
steps: Place a DNS resolver cache before a CloudFront object cache and label their independent TTLs.
Explain why changing a Route 53 record does not automatically purge an already cached object.

tasks.name: Calculate a freshness bound
steps: Assume an object was cached at 12:00 with an effective TTL of 300 seconds, with no invalidation or early eviction.
At 12:03 its modeled remaining freshness is 120 seconds. This simplified bound does not describe browser caches or every edge location.

tasks.name: Audit a cache key
steps: Two authenticated users request /profile and the origin returns different private content. The proposed cache key contains only the path.
Reject shared caching unless a correctly reviewed design prevents cross-user reuse; forwarding authorization alone is not proof of isolation.

tasks.name: Plan a safe asset release
steps: Publish app.v2.js under a new versioned name in a hypothetical release, then update the HTML reference with a deliberately short freshness policy.
Keep app.v1.js during rollback. Offline reasoning does not validate real DNS propagation, bucket policy, or cache behavior.

key_terms: TTL: allowed cache freshness duration.
Cache key: request attributes identifying a reusable response.
Origin: source contacted for uncached content.
Invalidation: request to remove cached objects.
Alias record: Route 53 integration pointing to supported targets.
lesson.safety: Do not edit DNS or distributions. Requests, transfer, invalidations, logs, and origin fetches may cost money; never cache real private profiles for experimentation.
cleanup: Retain the cache-key and release decisions.
No public records or cached objects were changed.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, users see old JavaScript after a successful deployment. How would you distinguish DNS, edge-cache, and browser-cache causes?
interview_points: Inspect the resolved target and actual asset URL.
Review response cache headers and effective policy TTLs.
Use versioned assets and preserve rollback references.
Avoid assuming DNS changes invalidate content.

aws-platform/aws-route-53-and-cloudfront.core: Route 53 resolves names; CloudFront caches responses using a deliberate key and freshness policy. Diagnose DNS and content lifetimes separately, avoid sharing personalized data, and prefer versioned static assets.
objectives: Trace DNS and edge caches separately

storyboard.title: A CloudFront release serves an old asset
storyboard.objective: Connect object freshness to versioned recovery.

scenes.title: Cached asset served
scenes.caption: The same URL still identifies a fresh cached object.
scenes.narration: The browser reaches CloudFront and receives the cached asset because its effective freshness interval has not ended.

scenes.title: Origin update appears missing
scenes.caption: Deploying bytes does not force every cache to refresh.
scenes.narration: The origin changes under the same path while the edge still has a usable cached response, creating inconsistent release observations.

scenes.title: Use a new versioned URL
scenes.caption: Release references identify the intended artifact.
scenes.narration: Updated HTML references a new asset name, producing a distinct cache lookup while retaining the previous asset for rollback.

lesson.title: AWS SQS SNS EventBridge and delivery semantics
lesson.why: Messaging decouples services but introduces duplicate delivery, delayed processing, and replay decisions. Picking a service by popularity rather than delivery requirements makes failures surprising.
lesson.what: Distinguish durable work queues, publish-subscribe fan-out, and event routing. Design consumers around business idempotency and explicit failure retention.

concepts.name: SQS buffers work
concepts.body: SQS lets consumers receive messages independently of producers. Standard queues provide at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering. Visibility timeout hides received messages temporarily; successful processing must be followed by deletion, and duplicate delivery remains a possibility.

concepts.name: SNS distributes notifications
concepts.body: SNS publishes to subscriptions, enabling fan-out to queues and other supported endpoints. Each subscription has its own delivery behavior and filtering. A publish success is not proof that every downstream business transaction completed; subscriber isolation and failure handling remain necessary.

concepts.name: EventBridge routes structured events
concepts.body: EventBridge routes events through supported bus and target models. Classic rule-based buses match event patterns; newer bus options have distinct subscriber and retention semantics. Check the chosen model's retries and failure handling. Schema evolution can change which events match routing criteria.

concepts.name: Ordering does not remove idempotency
concepts.body: FIFO features constrain ordering and deduplication within documented scopes, such as message groups and deduplication windows. They do not automatically make an external database update exactly once. Consumer crashes between committing a side effect and acknowledging delivery create ambiguous outcomes.

e2e: Define event identity, schema version, ordering scope, and acceptable processing delay.
Choose queueing, fan-out, or event-pattern routing according to consumer relationships.
Set visibility, retry, retention, and dead-letter policies to match processing time.
Commit business effects using durable duplicate protection before acknowledging delivery.
Monitor oldest-message age and failures, then replay only after correcting the cause.

tasks.name: Choose a topology
steps: One image-processing job should reach one worker, while each order event must reach billing and analytics.
Choose a queue for worker competition and separate subscriber queues for fan-out so a slow analytics consumer does not block billing.

tasks.name: Calculate backlog growth
steps: Assume producers send 150 messages/second and consumers complete 110/second for five minutes.
Backlog grows by (150 - 110) x 300 = 12,000 messages, excluding retries. Increasing retention preserves work longer but does not create processing capacity.

tasks.name: Trace duplicate delivery
steps: A consumer writes order A to its database, then crashes before deleting the queue message.
On redelivery, check the stable order ID and existing completion state. Expected business result remains one order, not two.

tasks.name: Review a replay plan
steps: A schema change sent 200 synthetic events to a dead-letter queue. Fix parsing, test one event, then replay at a bounded rate.
Keep duplicate checks active. These mocks do not prove real service ordering, deduplication, or IAM behavior.

key_terms: Visibility timeout: temporary hiding of an in-flight queue message.
Fan-out: delivering an event to multiple independent consumers.
Event pattern: structured matching rule.
DLQ: retained destination for repeatedly failed delivery or processing.
Idempotency: repeated input has one intended logical effect.
lesson.safety: Do not publish real events. Messaging requests, retries, retention, and downstream actions may incur cost; replaying business events can trigger real financial or notification effects.
cleanup: Future test queues and subscriptions need explicit removal and retained-message review.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a consumer processed an order twice despite using a queue. Why is that possible and where should the fix live?
interview_points: Explain commit-before-acknowledgement ambiguity.
Use durable business idempotency.
Inspect source-specific retry and visibility controls.
Do not equate FIFO features with exactly-once external effects.

aws-platform/aws-sqs-sns-eventbridge-and.core: SQS buffers work, SNS fans out, and EventBridge routes events. Source-specific delivery semantics still require durable idempotency, bounded retries, and controlled replay. Queue depth grows when arrivals exceed completions.

storyboard.title: A queue redelivers an already committed order
storyboard.objective: Show the gap between delivery acknowledgement and business completion.

scenes.title: First delivery
scenes.caption: A business write precedes message deletion.
scenes.narration: The consumer receives a message and commits the order using a stable identifier in durable storage.

scenes.title: Consumer crashes
scenes.caption: The acknowledgement gap allows another delivery.
scenes.narration: The worker stops before deleting the message, so a later receive can expose the same order again.

scenes.title: Recognize prior completion
scenes.caption: Deduplication belongs at the business boundary.
scenes.narration: The recovered consumer checks durable completion state and acknowledges the duplicate without creating another order or payment.

lesson.title: AWS API Gateway and service integration
lesson.why: An API front door must do more than forward requests. Authentication, authorization, validation, integration permissions, timeouts, and client retries jointly determine safety and reliability.
lesson.what: Design a synthetic order API using API Gateway and a backend integration, distinguishing product choices and usage controls from real access control.

concepts.name: API types have different features
concepts.body: REST APIs, HTTP APIs, and WebSocket APIs support different integration and management features. Select from required authorization, protocol, transformation, and operational needs rather than assuming examples transfer unchanged. A stage and deployment determine which configuration clients actually invoke.

concepts.name: Authentication is not an API key
concepts.body: An API key used by a REST API usage plan identifies a client for metering and throttling; it is not a substitute for authentication and authorization. IAM, JWT-based options where supported, or authorizers establish identity and permitted access.

concepts.name: Integration has its own contract
concepts.body: Gateway-to-backend permissions, payload format, status mapping, and timeout behavior must agree with the backend. A gateway timeout does not prove the backend stopped or rolled back. Idempotency keys protect mutating operations when callers retry uncertain outcomes.

concepts.name: Throttles are not hard billing caps
concepts.body: Rate and burst controls limit traffic on a best-effort basis within documented scopes. Usage-plan quotas should not be treated as exact cost ceilings or security boundaries. Protect downstream capacity separately, and observe gateway errors and backend failures as distinct signals.

e2e: Specify request and response schemas, authentication, authorization, and versioning.
Choose the API type and integration model that support those requirements.
Scope invocation permissions and map errors without leaking backend internals.
Set bounded timeouts and client retry rules with idempotent mutation handling.
Test positive, unauthorized, malformed, throttled, and ambiguous-timeout scenarios before release.

tasks.name: Separate request gates
steps: Draw identity validation, resource authorization, schema validation, and usage tracking as separate checks.
Explain why possession of a usage-plan API key alone should not authorize reading another customer's order.

tasks.name: Model a token bucket
steps: Assume an illustrative limiter starts with 20 tokens and replenishes ten per second. Thirty simultaneous requests arrive before any refill.
Expected model: 20 admitted and ten limited. Actual API Gateway enforcement is best effort and distributed, so this is not a guaranteed quota test.

tasks.name: Trace a timeout
steps: An order backend commits after the gateway has timed out. The client resends the same order request.
Require a stable idempotency key and return the prior result where valid instead of creating another order.

tasks.name: Write a contract table
steps: Specify synthetic expected responses for missing identity, invalid body, forbidden order, and unavailable backend.
Keep errors non-sensitive and correlation IDs useful. Offline contracts do not validate actual gateway integration or IAM policy.

key_terms: Authorizer: component evaluating request identity or access.
Integration: gateway connection to a backend service.
Stage: named deployment environment.
Burst: short-term traffic allowance.
Idempotency key: identifier deduplicating equivalent mutations.
lesson.safety: Do not deploy or invoke an API. Gateway calls, backend work, logs, and abuse can incur charges; never log bearer tokens or personal request bodies.
cleanup: No API keys, stages, or endpoints were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a team claims usage-plan keys and quotas provide complete security and a fixed spend ceiling. What do you challenge?
interview_points: Keys identify metered clients, not complete authorization.
Best-effort throttles are not exact cost caps.
Protect backend capacity and redact logs.
Handle timeout retries with business idempotency.

aws-platform/aws-api-gateway-and-service.core: API Gateway integrates protocol, identity, validation, and backend invocation. Usage-plan keys are not authentication, throttles are not exact spend caps, and gateway timeouts do not establish transaction failure.
objectives: Separate API access and usage controls

storyboard.title: An API timeout hides a committed order
storyboard.objective: Show why retries need an idempotency contract.

scenes.title: Validated request forwarded
scenes.caption: Identity and payload gates precede integration.
scenes.narration: The gateway accepts an authorized order request and forwards its stable idempotency key to the backend.

scenes.title: Gateway wait expires
scenes.caption: The backend may still complete the write.
scenes.narration: The client receives a timeout while the backend continues processing, leaving the client uncertain about the order's outcome.

scenes.title: Retry returns existing result
scenes.caption: The same key identifies the earlier operation.
scenes.narration: The client retries under a bounded policy, and the backend recognizes the existing order rather than repeating the mutation.

lesson.title: AWS Step Functions orchestration
lesson.why: A workflow that spans several services cannot rely on one database transaction to undo everything. Orchestration makes progress visible, but retries and compensation still require business design.
lesson.what: Model a reservation workflow with Step Functions states, bounded retries, catches, and compensation. Choose Standard or Express using documented execution semantics rather than a generic serverless label.

concepts.name: State machines make control explicit
concepts.body: Task states invoke work, Choice states branch, and Wait states delay progression without a busy loop. Inputs and outputs form a data contract between states. Keep payloads small and store large artifacts externally using appropriately protected references.

concepts.name: Workflow types are not interchangeable
concepts.body: Standard supports durable long-running workflows and execution history; Express targets shorter high-volume processing with different execution semantics and observability. Asynchronous Express is at-least-once, while synchronous Express has different guarantees. Check integration support and limits for the selected type.

concepts.name: Retry handles specific transient failures
concepts.body: Retry rules match errors with bounded attempts and backoff; Catch routes failures to explicit handling. A Task can have committed an external effect before its response is lost. Even with Standard's execution model, configured retries and ambiguous integrations require idempotent business operations.

concepts.name: Compensation is not rollback magic
concepts.body: A saga uses explicit compensating actions, such as releasing inventory after payment failure. Compensation may fail, and some effects cannot be fully reversed. Persist correlation identifiers and provide an operator path for partially completed work rather than declaring every failed workflow harmless.

e2e: Define each business step, its input contract, and its independently observable effect.
Select workflow type from duration, volume, integration, and delivery requirements.
Add error-specific bounded retries and catches around external operations.
Define compensation and manual recovery for each irreversible or uncertain transition.
Review execution history and business state together before replaying a failed workflow.

tasks.name: Sketch a reservation saga
steps: Draw reserve inventory, charge payment, and confirm order, with release inventory on payment failure.
Label payment and reservation identifiers needed to correlate retries and compensation.

tasks.name: Calculate retry delay
steps: Assume three retry delays starting at two seconds and doubling: 2, 4, and 8 seconds.
Expected waiting time is 14 seconds, excluding task runtimes and jitter. A retry budget must include all of these terms to satisfy an end-to-end deadline.

tasks.name: Handle an uncertain charge
steps: A payment provider processes a charge but the task response is lost. Preserve the same provider-supported idempotency key when retrying.
Do not claim that workflow-level execution guarantees alone prove exactly-once charging.

tasks.name: Design failed compensation handling
steps: Payment fails and inventory release also fails. Route to a recoverable incident state with order and reservation IDs rather than silently ending success.
This mock state machine does not execute real service integrations or prove IAM permissions.

key_terms: State machine: explicit model of workflow transitions.
Task: state performing external work.
Catch: transition handling a matched error.
Backoff: increasing delay between attempts.
Compensation: business action mitigating an earlier committed effect.
lesson.safety: Do not execute workflows. State transitions or Express duration, integration calls, logs, and repeated downstream work may be billable; use no real payment identifiers.
cleanup: Keep the saga and retry budget.
Discard synthetic execution IDs; no state machines or logs were created.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a Standard workflow retries a payment task after a timeout. Why should the task still use a payment idempotency key?
interview_points: The external effect may have committed before response loss.
Configured retries can repeat task work.
Workflow semantics do not atomically include every external system.
Track compensation and unresolved partial state explicitly.

aws-platform/aws-step-functions-orchestr.core: Step Functions makes control flow durable and observable, not every business operation atomic. Select Standard/Express deliberately, bound retries, retain idempotency keys, and treat compensation as fallible work.

storyboard.title: Payment failure triggers a reservation compensation
storyboard.objective: Show explicit recovery rather than imaginary distributed rollback.

scenes.title: Reserve then charge
scenes.caption: The workflow coordinates distinct committed effects.
scenes.narration: Inventory is reserved before the workflow requests payment, preserving identifiers that link each step to the same order.

scenes.title: Payment cannot complete
scenes.caption: A failed task leaves earlier work to resolve.
scenes.narration: Bounded retries exhaust for a known payment failure, so the workflow enters a recovery branch rather than assuming inventory disappeared.

scenes.title: Compensate explicitly
scenes.caption: Release has its own success and failure handling.
scenes.narration: The workflow requests inventory release and records its outcome; unresolved compensation remains visible for controlled operator recovery.

lesson.title: AWS CloudWatch CloudTrail and Config
lesson.why: Metrics can reveal an outage without explaining who changed a setting. Audit events can identify a caller without measuring customer impact. These evidence types answer different questions.
lesson.what: Combine CloudWatch operational telemetry, CloudTrail activity records, and AWS Config resource history in a fictional deployment investigation.

concepts.name: CloudWatch measures operation
concepts.body: Metrics, logs, dashboards, and alarms help observe resource and application behavior. An alarm depends on period, statistic, evaluation windows, and missing-data treatment. Average latency can hide tail failures, while high-cardinality custom metrics can increase both cost and analytical complexity.

concepts.name: CloudTrail records activity
concepts.body: CloudTrail captures supported account actions as events. Event history provides recent regional management-event history; data events require appropriate configuration and may incur additional charges. Absence from a default view is not proof that no object access or application action occurred.

concepts.name: Config records resource state
concepts.body: AWS Config tracks supported resource configurations when recording is configured and evaluates rules for compliance. A compliant evaluation means the resource matches that rule's criteria, not that the application is healthy or universally secure. Scope and recording coverage must be documented.

concepts.name: Correlation needs time and identity
concepts.body: Normalize timestamps, resource IDs, request IDs, and deployment versions when building an incident timeline. Delayed delivery and incomplete collection can leave gaps. Preserve original evidence and separate observations from hypotheses instead of presenting a plausible sequence as proven causality.

e2e: Define service-level signals and collect appropriately scoped metrics and redacted logs.
Configure activity and configuration recording needed for the investigation requirements.
Detect an impact signal and establish a time window with clock assumptions.
Correlate changes, caller identities, configuration states, and application outcomes.
Verify the proposed cause with a bounded test or rollback and record remaining evidence gaps.

tasks.name: Choose the evidence source
steps: Map rising 5xx rate, who changed a security group, and the group's earlier configuration to operational telemetry, CloudTrail, and Config respectively.
Document that collection scope determines whether the desired evidence actually exists.

tasks.name: Calculate an error ratio
steps: Synthetic counts show 75 failed requests out of 5,000 in five minutes. Expected error ratio is 75 / 5,000 x 100 = 1.5%.
Compare with a hypothetical 1% alert threshold; do not average unrelated host percentages to obtain the service ratio.

tasks.name: Challenge missing evidence
tasks.goal: Avoid claims from an empty search.
steps: A default management-event search shows no S3 object download. Explain why data-event configuration and search scope must be checked.
Absence of this event in that view is not evidence of absence of access.

tasks.name: Build a causal timeline
steps: Order synthetic events: deployment at 10:00, configuration change at 10:02, errors at 10:03, rollback at 10:08.
Propose one confirming observation and one competing explanation. Offline records do not prove any real incident or IAM behavior.

key_terms: Metric: numerical observation over time.
Management event: recorded control-plane activity.
Data event: recorded resource-data operation where supported.
Configuration item: recorded resource-state representation.
Evaluation window: observations considered by an alarm.
lesson.safety: Use fabricated telemetry only. Log ingestion, retention, queries, custom metrics, data events, and configuration recording can cost money; never include credentials or private payloads.
cleanup: Future tests must remove unnecessary alarms and explicitly retain or delete logs according to policy.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a dashboard is red but Config says compliant. Can both be correct?
interview_points: Operational health and rule compliance measure different properties.
Inspect exact rule scope and telemetry definitions.
Correlate activity and configuration changes.
State collection gaps and avoid claiming causality from timestamps alone.

aws-platform/aws-cloudwatch-cloudtrail-a.core: CloudWatch observes behavior, CloudTrail records supported activity, and Config tracks supported configuration. Collection coverage, timestamps, and identifiers determine what conclusions the evidence can support.

storyboard.title: A configuration change coincides with errors
storyboard.objective: Join different evidence types without treating correlation as proof.

scenes.title: Baseline evidence
scenes.caption: Telemetry and configuration describe a healthy period.
scenes.narration: The investigator records the earlier resource state and normal request-error ratio with a shared time reference.

scenes.title: Errors follow a change
scenes.caption: A caller event suggests a hypothesis, not proof.
scenes.narration: CloudTrail identifies a configuration action near the error increase, while Config helps reconstruct which resource settings changed.

scenes.caption: Recovery evidence and competing causes remain important.

lesson.title: AWS KMS Secrets Manager and certificate management
lesson.why: Encryption keys, application secrets, and TLS certificates have different lifecycles. Confusing rotation with replacement or deleting an old key can make retained data permanently unreadable.
lesson.what: Map KMS envelope encryption, Secrets Manager credential rotation, and certificate renewal into an offline application dependency plan.

concepts.name: KMS controls key operations
concepts.body: Envelope encryption uses a data key for bulk data and protects that key with a KMS key. Key policies and IAM authorization govern access. KMS key rotation is not the same as reencrypting every stored object; retained encrypted data can still depend on earlier key material.

concepts.name: Secrets Manager stores changing credentials
concepts.body: A secret can have versions and staging labels used during rotation. Rotation must update both the secret value and the target service credential in a coordinated manner. Managed rotation and Lambda-based rotation apply to different supported scenarios; applications must refresh cached credentials safely.

concepts.name: Certificates bind names to keys
concepts.body: TLS validation checks hostname, trust chain, and validity period. AWS Certificate Manager supports managed certificate workflows for eligible integrations, but imported certificates and deployment locations require separate lifecycle review. Issuance alone does not prove the active listener serves the new certificate.

concepts.name: Recovery needs dependency mapping
concepts.body: Backups encrypted under a key need that key available during restore. Disabling or scheduling deletion of a key can break data recovery, while rotating a database credential can break stale connection pools. Retain auditable access, expiry alerts, and controlled rollback procedures without exposing secret values.

e2e: Inventory which data, credentials, certificates, and backups depend on each key or secret.
Scope retrieval and cryptographic permissions separately from administration.
Plan rotation stages and application refresh behavior with a synthetic validation account.
Verify target authentication and served TLS identity after any approved change.
Retain required old material and recovery access until dependency and retention checks permit removal.

tasks.name: Classify three assets
tasks.goal: Avoid using one lifecycle for everything.
steps: Map an encrypted data key, database password, and HTTPS certificate to encryption, authentication, and server identity roles.
Identify the systems that must change or remain available when each is rotated.

tasks.name: Work a rotation timeline
steps: Assume clients cache a password for 15 minutes, but a hypothetical rotation revokes the old password after five minutes.
The possible stale-client failure window is ten minutes. Reduce cache lifetime or use an appropriate coordinated overlap strategy; do not assume every database supports two passwords.

tasks.name: Protect historical recovery
steps: A 90-day backup still depends on a KMS key proposed for deletion next week.
Reject deletion until dependencies and retention obligations are resolved. Rotating the key is not equivalent to making old encrypted backups independent of it.

tasks.name: Verify certificate deployment
steps: Write an offline checklist for hostname, chain, expiry, listener association, and renewal eligibility.
Use no private keys or real secret values. The checklist does not prove live certificate deployment or cloud authorization.

key_terms: Envelope encryption: data encryption with a separately protected data key.
Key policy: authorization policy attached to a KMS key.
Secret version: retained revision of a secret value.
Rotation: coordinated replacement of active credentials or key material.
Certificate chain: trust path from server certificate to trusted issuer.
lesson.safety: Do not retrieve secrets, rotate credentials, or delete keys. KMS requests, stored secrets, rotation integrations, and certificate options can incur charges; key deletion can be irreversible.
cleanup: Retain only names of fictional dependencies.
Remove synthetic credential examples; never copy real secret material into lesson notes.
lesson.interview_question: Hypothetically, a team wants to delete an old encryption key immediately after rotation. What evidence is required first?
interview_points: Map ciphertext and backup dependencies.
Distinguish rotation from re-encryption.
Verify recovery access and retention obligations.
Use approved deletion safeguards rather than assuming old means unused.

aws-platform/aws-kms-secrets-manager-and.core: KMS keys protect cryptographic operations, Secrets Manager coordinates credential values, and certificates establish TLS identity. Rotation must account for caches, target updates, and historical recovery dependencies.

storyboard.title: A credential rotation encounters stale clients
storyboard.objective: Connect secret version changes to target authentication.

scenes.title: Current credentials work
scenes.caption: Application and target agree on the active credential.
scenes.narration: The application retrieves the current secret version and uses it to establish an authorized database connection.

scenes.title: Cache outlives rotation overlap
scenes.caption: A stored credential can become stale.
scenes.narration: Rotation updates the target, but a client still holds an old password and fails when opening a new connection.

scenes.title: Coordinate refresh and validation
scenes.caption: Rotation success includes application authentication.
scenes.narration: The client refreshes its credential under the approved rotation design and validates a new connection without logging the secret.
